subproblems.title: Lower Lipschitz bound for a C¹ map near a point where its derivative is injective
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, let G : ℝ^n → ℝ^P be a C¹ map and let x ∈ ℝ^n be a point at which the derivative DG(x) : ℝ^n → ℝ^P is injective. Then there are δ > 0 and μ > 0 such that μ|a − b| ≤ |G(a) − G(b)| for all a, b in the open ball B_δ(x). Here ℝ^k = Euclid k carries the Euclidean norm |·|.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (G : Euclid n → Euclid P) (x : Euclid n), ContDiff ℝ 1 G → Injective (fderiv ℝ G x) → ∃ δ μ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ 0 < μ ∧ ∀ a ∈ ball x δ, ∀ b ∈ ball x δ, μ * ‖a - b‖ ≤ ‖G a - G b‖
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Step 5 of the parent proof of Simon Ch. 3, Lemma 1.2 (chapter-03.txt lines 25–66; the 'only if' part is lines 39–65).
- The printed proof says: if the Jacobian of G_{ij} is non-zero at x, then for some ρ > 0 the set G_{ij}(B_ρ(x)) is an n-dimensional C¹ submanifold of ℝ^{n+ℓ}, with G_{ij} as a local representation. (Erratum: the book prints ℝ^n.)
- The parent proof records the quantitative content of this inverse-function argument as a lower Lipschitz bound on a ball. That bound is the present statement, for a single C¹ map G.
- A non-zero Jacobian J_G(x) = √det(DG(x)* DG(x)) means exactly that DG(x) is injective.
Notation: |·| is the Euclidean norm, ‖A‖ the operator norm of a linear map A, and B_δ(x) the open ball.

1. (Coercivity of L.) Put L := DG(x), an injective linear map ℝ^n → ℝ^P.
- Since ℝ^n is finite-dimensional, L is a linear isomorphism of ℝ^n onto the subspace L(ℝ^n). Its inverse L(ℝ^n) → ℝ^n is linear on a finite-dimensional normed space, hence bounded.
- So there is N > 0 with |v| ≤ N|Lv| for every v ∈ ℝ^n. (Equivalently: if n ≥ 1, v ↦ |Lv| is continuous and positive on the compact unit sphere, so it has a positive minimum. If n = 0, every v is 0 and any N > 0 works.)
- Put μ := 1/(2N) > 0. Then |Lv| ≥ |v|/N = 2μ|v| for all v ∈ ℝ^n.
2. (Continuity of DG at x.) G is C¹, so y ↦ DG(y) is continuous from ℝ^n into the linear maps ℝ^n → ℝ^P with the operator norm, in particular at x. Choose δ > 0 with ‖DG(y) − L‖ ≤ μ for all y ∈ B_δ(x).
3. (Mean value inequality.) Let φ(y) := G(y) − L(y).
- Since L is linear, φ is differentiable at every y with Dφ(y) = DG(y) − L. So ‖Dφ(y)‖ ≤ μ for y ∈ B_δ(x).
- The ball B_δ(x) is convex, so the mean value inequality gives |φ(a) − φ(b)| ≤ μ|a − b| for all a, b ∈ B_δ(x).
- Since L is linear, φ(a) − φ(b) = G(a) − G(b) − L(a − b). Hence |G(a) − G(b) − L(a − b)| ≤ μ|a − b|.
4. (Conclusion.) Let a, b ∈ B_δ(x). By the triangle inequality and steps 1 and 3,
 |G(a) − G(b)| ≥ |L(a − b)| − |G(a) − G(b) − L(a − b)| ≥ 2μ|a − b| − μ|a − b| = μ|a − b|.
So δ > 0 and μ > 0 have the required property. ∎

Implementation note (not part of the mathematics). No extra import is needed.
- Step 1: apply LinearMap.injective_iff_antilipschitz to (fderiv ℝ G x : Euclid n →ₗ[ℝ] Euclid P). This gives N > 0 with AntilipschitzWith N. ZeroHomClass.bound_of_antilipschitz then gives ‖v‖ ≤ N * ‖L v‖.
- Steps 2–3 together say that G approximates L with constant μ near x, which is strict differentiability:
  - hG.contDiffAt.hasStrictFDerivAt (by norm_num) : HasStrictFDerivAt G (fderiv ℝ G x) x.
  - HasStrictFDerivAt.approximates_deriv_on_nhds with c := ⟨μ, hμ.le⟩ gives s ∈ 𝓝 x with ApproximatesLinearOn G L s c. This means ‖G a - G b - L (a - b)‖ ≤ μ * ‖a - b‖ for a, b ∈ s; apply it as happrox a ha b hb.

proof_key_steps: L := DG(x) is injective on the finite-dimensional ℝ^n, so there is N > 0 with |v| ≤ N|Lv|. Put μ := 1/(2N), so |Lv| ≥ 2μ|v| for all v.
Since G is C¹, DG is continuous at x. This gives δ > 0 with ‖DG(y) − L‖ ≤ μ on B_δ(x); equivalently, use strict differentiability at x.
The mean value inequality for G − L on the convex ball gives |G(a) − G(b) − L(a − b)| ≤ μ|a − b| for a, b ∈ B_δ(x).
By the triangle inequality, |G(a) − G(b)| ≥ 2μ|a − b| − μ|a − b| = μ|a − b| on B_δ(x).

subproblems.title: A C¹ image is covered, up to an H^n-null set, by countably many images of balls carrying lower Lipschitz bounds
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ and let G : ℝ^n → ℝ^P be a C¹ map. Then there are points c_k ∈ ℝ^n, reals r_k and constants m_k > 0 (k ∈ ℕ) with two properties. (i) m_k|a − b| ≤ |G(a) − G(b)| for all a, b in the open ball B_{r_k}(c_k), which is empty when r_k ≤ 0. (ii) H^n(G(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_k G(B_{r_k}(c_k))) = 0, where H^n = μHE[n] on ℝ^P.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (G : Euclid n → Euclid P), ContDiff ℝ 1 G → ∃ (c : ℕ → Euclid n) (r m : ℕ → ℝ), (∀ k, 0 < m k) ∧ (∀ k, ∀ a ∈ ball (c k) (r k), ∀ b ∈ ball (c k) (r k), m k * ‖a - b‖ ≤ ‖G a - G b‖) ∧ μHE[n] (range G \ ⋃ k, G '' ball (c k) (r k)) = 0
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Simon Ch. 3, Lemma 1.2, 'only if' part (chapter-03.txt lines 39–65 within the lemma at lines 25–66), final paragraph (lines 61–65), as expanded in steps 4, 6 and 7 of the parent proof. Here it is stated for a single C¹ map G; the book's G is G_{ij}.
The printed text makes three claims:
- By the area formula, the image of the zero set of the Jacobian is null.
- At a point x where the Jacobian is non-zero, there is ρ > 0 such that G(B_ρ(x)) is an n-dimensional C¹ submanifold.
- So the image is a null set together with countably many such submanifolds.
Corrections to the printed proof, as in the parent proof:
- The garbled 'by the area formula L^n({x : J_{G_{ij}} = 0}' should read H^n(G_{ij}({J_{G_{ij}} = 0})) = 0.
- The local pieces are submanifolds of ℝ^{n+ℓ} = ℝ^P; the book prints ℝ^n.
As in the parent proof:
- Each local piece is recorded quantitatively by a lower Lipschitz bound on an open ball.
- The countable (Lindelöf) selection uses balls with centres in a dense sequence and radii 1/(p + 1).
Notation: H^n = μHE[n]; B_ρ(x) is the open ball, empty when ρ ≤ 0.

1. (The critical image is null.) Let C := {x ∈ ℝ^n : DG(x) is not injective}.
- G is C¹, hence differentiable everywhere. So C = {x : G is differentiable at x and DG(x) is not injective}.
- This is exactly the set where the Jacobian J_G(x) = √det(DG(x)* DG(x)) vanishes. By the area formula, H^n(G(C)) = 0. In detail:
  - If n > P, then H^n vanishes identically on ℝ^P, so there is nothing to prove.
  - Let n ≤ P. The injective linear maps ℝ^n → ℝ^P form an open set and DG is continuous, so C is closed.
  - Fix R ∈ ℕ and put A_R := C ∩ closedBall(0, R), a compact and hence Lebesgue-measurable set. G is C¹, so it is Lipschitz on the compact convex set closedBall(0, R) (bounded derivative plus the mean value inequality), and hence on A_R. Also J_G = 0 on A_R.
  - The general area formula (Simon Ch. 2, 3.4, for Lipschitz maps from measurable subsets of ℝ^n into ℝ^P with P ≥ n) gives ∫_{ℝ^P} H^0(G^{-1}(y) ∩ A_R) dH^n(y) = ∫_{A_R} J_G dL^n = 0. (The book text of 3.4 prints dH^m(y), a misprint for dH^n(y).)
  - The multiplicity H^0(G^{-1}(y) ∩ A_R) is ≥ 1 on the compact (hence Borel) set G(A_R). So H^n(G(A_R)) = 0.
  - Finally G(C) = ⋃_R G(A_R), so H^n(G(C)) = 0.
- In SimonGMT this is Chapter02.area_image_criticalSet_eq_zero. It holds for every map f : E → F between finite-dimensional real inner product spaces, is stated for μHE[finrank ℝ E], and here finrank ℝ ℝ^n = n. SimonGMT proves it by applying the injective area formula to the lifted maps x ↦ (G(x), εx) and letting ε ↓ 0.
2. (Candidate balls.) ℝ^n is separable and non-empty, so there is a sequence (e_q)_{q∈ℕ} dense in ℝ^n.
- For q, p ∈ ℕ put β_{q,p} := B_{1/(p+1)}(e_q).
- Call β_{q,p} good if there is μ > 0 with μ|a − b| ≤ |G(a) − G(b)| for all a, b ∈ β_{q,p}.
3. (Enumeration.) Fix a bijection ℕ → ℕ × ℕ, k ↦ (q_k, p_k), and write pair(q, p) for its inverse; for instance Mathlib's Nat.unpair with inverse Nat.pair. Put c_k := e_{q_k}.
- If β_{q_k,p_k} is good, put r_k := 1/(p_k + 1), and let m_k > 0 be a witness of goodness (chosen by the axiom of choice).
- Otherwise put r_k := 0 and m_k := 1.
4. (Positivity and (i).) In both cases m_k > 0.
- If β_{q_k,p_k} is good, then B_{r_k}(c_k) = β_{q_k,p_k}. By the choice of the witness, m_k|a − b| ≤ |G(a) − G(b)| for all a, b in it.
- Otherwise B_{r_k}(c_k) = B_0(c_k) = ∅, and (i) holds vacuously.
5. (Every regular point lies in one of the balls.) Let x ∉ C, so DG(x) is injective.
- By the sibling lemma local_lower_lipschitz, applied to G and x, there are δ > 0 and μ > 0 with μ|a − b| ≤ |G(a) − G(b)| for all a, b ∈ B_δ(x).
- By the Archimedean property choose p ∈ ℕ with 1/(p + 1) < δ/2. By density choose q ∈ ℕ with |x − e_q| < 1/(p + 1). Then x ∈ β_{q,p}.
- For a ∈ β_{q,p}, |a − x| ≤ |a − e_q| + |e_q − x| < 2/(p + 1) < δ. So β_{q,p} ⊆ B_δ(x), and μ witnesses that β_{q,p} is good.
- For k := pair(q, p) we have (q_k, p_k) = (q, p), so c_k = e_q and r_k = 1/(p + 1). Hence x ∈ B_{r_k}(c_k).
6. ((ii), covering.) Let y ∈ G(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_k G(B_{r_k}(c_k)), say y = G(x).
- If x ∉ C, step 5 gives k with x ∈ B_{r_k}(c_k). Then y ∈ G(B_{r_k}(c_k)), a contradiction. Hence x ∈ C and y ∈ G(C).
- Therefore G(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_k G(B_{r_k}(c_k)) ⊆ G(C).
- By monotonicity of the measure and step 1, H^n(G(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_k G(B_{r_k}(c_k))) ≤ H^n(G(C)) = 0. ∎

Implementation note (not part of the mathematics).
- Step 1 needs `import Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter02.AreaCritical`. The module is prebuilt and compiles together with the frozen contract.
  - Use Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter02.area_image_criticalSet_eq_zero G, rewritten with finrank_euclideanSpace_fin.
  - Use ContDiff.differentiable (by norm_num) for the differentiability conjunct.
- Other lemmas: TopologicalSpace.exists_dense_seq, DenseRange.exists_dist_lt, exists_nat_one_div_lt, half_pos, dist_triangle, Nat.pair, Nat.unpair, Nat.unpair_pair, ball_zero, Set.notMem_empty and measure_mono_null.
- Use `classical` for the if/dite on goodness, and Exists.choose / Exists.choose_spec for the witness.
- The sibling enters as Submission.codim1_rdo_c1cov_local_lower_lipschitz P n G x hG hinj.
proof_key_steps: Let C = {x : DG(x) not injective}. By the area formula (SimonGMT area_image_criticalSet_eq_zero), H^n(G(C)) = 0.
Fix a dense sequence (e_q) and candidate balls β_{q,p} = B_{1/(p+1)}(e_q). A ball is good if it admits a lower Lipschitz constant μ > 0.

Enumerate (q,p) by a bijection ℕ → ℕ × ℕ (Nat.unpair, inverse Nat.pair). Good balls get r_k = 1/(p_k+1) and a witness m_k > 0. The others get r_k = 0 and m_k = 1, so the ball is empty and the bound is vacuous.

For x ∉ C, local_lower_lipschitz gives B_δ(x) with constant μ. Choose p with 2/(p+1) < δ and q with |x − e_q| < 1/(p+1). Then β_{q,p} contains x, is good, and lies in B_δ(x), so x ∈ B_{r_k}(c_k) for k = pair(q,p).
Hence G(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_k G(B_{r_k}(c_k)) ⊆ G(C), which is H^n-null.

subproblems.title: The image of an open ball under a C¹ map is Borel and has finite H^n measure
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, let g : ℝ^n → ℝ^P be a C¹ map, c ∈ ℝ^n and r ∈ ℝ. Then the image g(B_r(c)) of the open ball, which is empty if r ≤ 0, is a Borel subset of ℝ^P, and H^n(g(B_r(c))) < ∞, where H^n = μHE[n].
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (g : Euclid n → Euclid P) (c : Euclid n) (r : ℝ), ContDiff ℝ 1 g → MeasurableSet (g '' ball c r) ∧ μHE[n] (g '' ball c r) ≠ ∞
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Step 8 of the parent proof, i.e. properties (ii) and (iii) of the pieces N_k = g_k(B_{r_k}(c_k)), in the setting of Simon Ch. 3, Lemma 1.2 (chapter-03.txt lines 25–66).
- That lemma's proof uses that C¹ maps are Lipschitz on each closed ball.
- The measure bound is Simon Ch. 2, Theorem 1.8(i): H^m(f(A)) ≤ (Lip f)^m H^m(A). The book notes that this part of the argument is valid even if A is not H^m-measurable.
Notation: H^n = μHE[n], which equals Lebesgue measure L^n (volume) on ℝ^n. B_r(c) is the open ball and closedBall(c, ρ) the closed ball; both are empty for negative radius.

1. (Exhaustion of the open ball.) For t ∈ ℕ put ρ_t := r − 1/(t + 1). Then B_r(c) = ⋃_{t∈ℕ} closedBall(c, ρ_t).
- If |y − c| < r, the Archimedean property gives t with 1/(t + 1) < r − |y − c|, so |y − c| ≤ ρ_t.
- Conversely, |y − c| ≤ ρ_t implies |y − c| < r.
2. ((ii) Borel.) Hence g(B_r(c)) = ⋃_t g(closedBall(c, ρ_t)).
- Each closed ball of ℝ^n is compact (Heine–Borel), and g is continuous, being C¹.
- So each g(closedBall(c, ρ_t)) is compact, hence closed in the metric space ℝ^P, hence Borel.
- A countable union of Borel sets is Borel, so g(B_r(c)) is Borel.
3. (g is Lipschitz on the ball.) closedBall(c, r) is compact and convex.
- Dg is continuous, so it is bounded on this compact set, say ‖Dg(y)‖ ≤ Λ there.
- By the mean value inequality on the convex set, |g(a) − g(b)| ≤ Λ|a − b| for all a, b ∈ closedBall(c, r).
- In particular g is Λ-Lipschitz on B_r(c) ⊆ closedBall(c, r). If r < 0, both sets are empty and the claim is trivial.
4. ((iii) Finite measure.) By Simon Ch. 2, 1.8(i), applied to g restricted to B_r(c), H^n(g(B_r(c))) ≤ Λ^n H^n(B_r(c)), where H^n on the right is the measure on ℝ^n.
- On ℝ^n, H^n = μHE[n] equals Lebesgue measure.
- B_r(c) is bounded, so L^n(B_r(c)) < ∞.
- Hence H^n(g(B_r(c))) ≤ Λ^n L^n(B_r(c)) < ∞. ∎

Implementation note (not part of the mathematics). No extra import is needed.
- Steps 1–2: exists_nat_one_div_lt, image_iUnion, isCompact_closedBall, IsCompact.image (with hg.continuous), IsCompact.isClosed, IsClosed.measurableSet and MeasurableSet.iUnion.
- Step 3: ContDiffOn.exists_lipschitzOnWith (hg.contDiffOn) (by norm_num) (convex_closedBall c r) (isCompact_closedBall c r), then LipschitzOnWith.mono ball_subset_closedBall.
- Step 4:
  - Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter02.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image_le_of_lipschitzOn n, available through the contract's import of Chapter03.Rectifiable.
  - EuclideanSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume, measure_ball_lt_top, ENNReal.mul_ne_top, ENNReal.pow_ne_top and ne_top_of_le_ne_top.
proof_key_steps: B_r(c) = ⋃_t closedBall(c, r − 1/(t+1)), by the Archimedean property.
g is continuous, so each g(closedBall) is compact, hence closed and Borel. The countable union g(B_r(c)) is therefore Borel.
g is C¹ on the compact convex set closedBall(c, r), so it is Λ-Lipschitz there (bounded derivative plus the mean value inequality).
By Simon 2.1.8(i), H^n(g(B_r(c))) ≤ Λ^n H^n(B_r(c)) = Λ^n L^n(B_r(c)) < ∞.

subproblems.title: Given scalar C¹ approximation, a Lipschitz image is covered by countably many C¹ images up to an H^n-null set (Simon Ch. 3, 1.2, display (1))
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ. Assume (H): for every Lipschitz f : ℝ^n → ℝ (with a constant K ≥ 0) and every ε ∈ (0, ∞], there is a C¹ function g : ℝ^n → ℝ with L^n({x : f(x) ≠ g(x) or Df(x) ≠ Dg(x)}) < ε. Here L^n = volume and D is Mathlib's fderiv. (H) is the frozen statement of the sibling codim1_rdo_c1_approximation at dimension n (Simon Ch. 2, Theorem 1.5). Then for every Lipschitz map F : ℝ^n → ℝ^P there are C¹ maps G_i : ℝ^n → ℝ^P (i ∈ ℕ) with H^n(F(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_i G_i(ℝ^n)) = 0, where H^n = μHE[n].

Source. Simon Ch. 3, Lemma 1.2, 'only if' part (chapter-03.txt lines 39–65 within the lemma at lines 25–66), first half (lines 39–52), as expanded in steps 2 and 3 of the parent proof. Here it is stated for a single Lipschitz map F; the book's F is F_j.
The printed argument:
- By the C¹ Approximation Theorem 1.5 of Ch. 2, choose C¹ functions G_{1j}, G_{2j}, … with H^n({x : F_j(x) ≠ G_{ij}(x)}) < 1/i.
- Then Z_j = ℝ^n ∖ ⋃_i {x : F_j(x) = G_{ij}(x)} has H^n(Z_j) = 0. This gives display (1), with E_j = F_j(Z_j).
- H^n(E_j) = 0 because F_j is Lipschitz.
Corrections to the printed proof, as in the parent proof:
- The G_{ij} take values in ℝ^{n+ℓ} = ℝ^P; the book prints ℝ^ℓ.
- Display (1) should read F_j(ℝ^n) ⊆ E_j ∪ ⋃_i G_{ij}(ℝ^n). The book text prints 'graph F_j ⊂ E_j ∩ (⋃_i G_{ij}(ℝ^n))', and both 'graph F_j' and '∩' are misprints. (In chapter-03.txt '\' encodes ∩ and '[' encodes ∪.)
- The scalar Theorem 2.1.5 is applied coordinatewise to the vector-valued F_j.
About the hypothesis (H):
- Theorem 2.1.5 enters only through (H), which is verbatim the frozen type of the sibling codim1_rdo_c1_approximation at dimension n.
- The parent discharges (H) with that theorem.
- It is a hypothesis here because children of this node cannot import the parent's sibling.
Notation: H^n = μHE[n], which equals L^n = volume on ℝ^n; D is the derivative (fderiv).

1. (Coordinates are Lipschitz.) Let K ≥ 0 be a Lipschitz constant of F. For l ∈ {1, …, P} put F^l(x) := (F(x))_l.
- In ℝ^P, |y_l − y'_l| ≤ |y − y'|. So |F^l(x) − F^l(x')| ≤ |F(x) − F(x')| ≤ K|x − x'|.
- Thus each F^l : ℝ^n → ℝ is K-Lipschitz.
2. (Coordinatewise C¹ approximation.) Fix i ∈ ℕ and put δ_i := ((i + 1)(P + 1))^{-1}, a positive finite number.
- For each l, apply (H) to F^l, K and ε := δ_i.
- This gives a C¹ function g_{i,l} : ℝ^n → ℝ with L^n({x : F^l(x) ≠ g_{i,l}(x) or DF^l(x) ≠ Dg_{i,l}(x)}) < δ_i.
3. (The maps G_i.) Define G_i(x) := (g_{i,1}(x), …, g_{i,P}(x)) ∈ ℝ^P. G_i is C¹: each coordinate is C¹, and ℝ^P ≅ ℝ^{Fin P} is a continuous linear equivalence, so a map into ℝ^P is C¹ iff all its coordinates are.
4. (The disagreement set is small.)
- If F(x) ≠ G_i(x), then some coordinate differs: F^l(x) ≠ g_{i,l}(x).
- So {x : F(x) ≠ G_i(x)} ⊆ ⋃_{l=1}^P {x : F^l(x) ≠ g_{i,l}(x) or DF^l(x) ≠ Dg_{i,l}(x)}.
- By finite subadditivity and step 2, L^n({F ≠ G_i}) ≤ P δ_i ≤ (P + 1) δ_i = (i + 1)^{-1}.
- For P = 0 the union is empty: ℝ^0 is a single point, so F(x) = G_i(x).
5. (Z is Lebesgue-null.) Let Z := ⋂_{i∈ℕ} {x : F(x) ≠ G_i(x)}.
- For every i, L^n(Z) ≤ L^n({F ≠ G_i}) ≤ (i + 1)^{-1}.
- Given ε > 0, choose i ≥ 1 with 1/i < ε. Then L^n(Z) ≤ (i + 1)^{-1} ≤ 1/i < ε.
- Hence L^n(Z) = 0.
6. (E := F(Z) is H^n-null.) F is K-Lipschitz, so by Simon Ch. 2, 1.8(i), H^n(F(Z)) ≤ K^n H^n(Z) = K^n L^n(Z) = 0. The middle equality uses H^n = L^n on ℝ^n. The inequality of 1.8(i) needs no measurability (the book remarks this after the proof), and in any case Z is a G_δ set, since F and the G_i are continuous.
7. (Covering: corrected display (1).) Let y ∈ F(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_i G_i(ℝ^n), say y = F(x).
- For every i, F(x) ≠ G_i(x), since otherwise y = G_i(x) ∈ G_i(ℝ^n). So x ∈ Z and y ∈ F(Z).
- Thus F(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_i G_i(ℝ^n) ⊆ F(Z).
- By monotonicity and step 6, H^n(F(ℝ^n) ∖ ⋃_i G_i(ℝ^n)) ≤ H^n(F(Z)) = 0.
- The maps G_i are C¹ by step 3. ∎
